		<title>Beyond The Specification: What Really Determines PCIe Retimer Reach?</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/beyond-the-specification-what-really-determines-pcie-retimer-reach/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/beyond-the-specification-what-really-determines-pcie-retimer-reach/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Paul Karazuba]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 15 Oct 2026 07:07:45 +0000</pubDate>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Multiple interacting factors span silicon design, controller intelligence, channel quality, and the transmission medium itself.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/beyond-the-specification-what-really-determines-pcie-retimer-reach/">Beyond The Specification: What Really Determines PCIe Retimer Reach?</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>As AI servers, storage platforms, networking equipment, and high-performance computing systems continue to scale, PCIe links are being pushed farther than ever before. System architects frequently ask a seemingly simple question: <i>how far can a PCIe retimer extend a connection</i>? Unfortunately, there is no single answer. The effective reach of a PCIe retimer is influenced by multiple interacting factors that span silicon design, controller intelligence, channel quality, and the transmission medium itself.</p>
<p>In trying to answer the question, many engineers may initially focus on the PCIe specification and associated channel loss budgets. While specification compliance is essential, real-world reach is often determined by how well a retimer performs beyond the minimum requirements. The difference between a retimer that merely passes compliance testing and one that consistently delivers reliable operation in production deployments can be substantial. Maximizing PCIe reach requires a system-level approach that considers every aspect of the signal path.</p>
<p>At the foundation of retimer reach lies the quality of the SerDes architecture. The SerDes serves as the electrical engine that receives, conditions, and retransmits high-speed signals. PCI-SIG specifications define channel-loss requirements that compliant devices must support. For example, designs are commonly expected to accommodate around 36 dB of insertion loss at Nyquist frequency. However, leading retimer vendors frequently engineer their products to tolerate 40 dB or even higher levels of channel loss.</p>
<p>Those additional decibels may sound insignificant, but they often translate directly into greater deployment flexibility. Additional margin allows designers to support longer PCB traces, extra connectors, more backplane transitions, and greater manufacturing variation. In large systems where every connector, cable, and via adds loss and reflection, the difference between supporting 36 and 40 dB can determine whether a design succeeds without modification or requires a costly board redesign.</p>
<p>The ability to achieve this additional margin depends on sophisticated signal-processing techniques embedded within the SerDes. Advanced equalization circuitry, highly optimized clock recovery algorithms, robust jitter tolerance, and adaptive receiver technologies all contribute to extending channel reach. As the industry moves through PCIe Gen6 and prepares for future generations, these capabilities become increasingly important because every speed increase reduces the available system margin.</p>
<p>While the analog performance of the SerDes establishes the foundation, controller intelligence frequently determines how well that foundation performs in real-world environments. Modern PCIe systems operate under conditions that are far more complicated than laboratory compliance tests. Temperature fluctuations, voltage variations, component aging, process variation, and interoperability challenges all affect link stability.</p>
<p>One particularly important capability is the handling of corner cases. Specifications cannot anticipate every possible combination of endpoint, root complex, cable, switch, and retimer implementation. Real-world deployments often uncover scenarios that sit at the edge of compliance boundaries. Retimers with sophisticated controller designs are better equipped to manage these situations without causing system instability. As a result, controller quality frequently becomes a major differentiator among retimer solutions that appear similar when viewed purely from a PHY performance perspective.</p>
<p>Closely related to controller intelligence is the concept of designing beyond the specification. Compliance testing validates that a device meets defined requirements, but interoperability in production systems often requires more than simple compliance. Different vendors may interpret implementation details differently, resulting in subtle variations during link training, equalization, recovery, or power-state transitions.</p>
<p>The most robust retimers are designed with these realities in mind. They include additional logic and protocol awareness to handle unusual behaviors, accommodate implementation differences, and recover gracefully from unexpected situations. This philosophy of engineering beyond the specification can significantly improve compatibility across diverse ecosystems. For hyperscale operators, server manufacturers, and storage vendors, successful interoperability often matters as much as raw signal-integrity performance.</p>
<p>Another factor that significantly influences practical reach is observability. As PCIe speeds increase, diagnosing link issues becomes more challenging. The ability to see what is happening within the channel can determine whether a link operates reliably or remains a persistent source of field failures.</p>
<p>Modern retimers increasingly include sophisticated diagnostic and monitoring capabilities. Engineers need visibility into link-training behavior, equalization status, signal quality, error statistics, lane margins, and environmental conditions. This information helps identify weak channels, optimize system performance, and accelerate root-cause analysis during deployment. Although diagnostics do not directly improve insertion-loss tolerance, they often increase achievable system reach by allowing engineers to discover and resolve issues that would otherwise remain hidden. In many deployments, better visibility effectively creates additional operational margin by enabling more informed tuning and troubleshooting.</p>
<p>No discussion of retimer reach would be complete without considering the quality of the transmission channel itself. Even the most advanced retimer cannot fully compensate for a poorly designed channel. PCB material selection, impedance control, via construction, connector quality, routing practices, and crosstalk management all influence signal integrity.</p>
<p>As signaling rates continue to climb, low-loss PCB materials become increasingly attractive because they reduce attenuation and preserve signal quality across longer distances. Likewise, careful connector and via design can dramatically improve channel performance. A high-quality channel allows the retimer to devote its equalization resources to extending reach rather than simply compensating for avoidable losses and reflections.</p>
<p>The transmission medium also plays a critical role. Within a chassis, PCB traces dominate the channel budget. Beyond the board, copper cables provide additional flexibility and enable connectivity to external accelerators, storage systems, and expansion modules. High-quality active copper assemblies can often extend PCIe connectivity to approximately two meters while maintaining acceptable performance. However, this capability depends heavily on cable construction, shielding effectiveness, copper quality, and connector design.</p>
<p>Looking forward, optical connectivity is poised to redefine expectations for PCIe reach. Emerging PCIe-over-optical implementations enable PCIe traffic to traverse fiber while maintaining standard PCIe operation. The implications are profound. Instead of being measured in centimeters of board traces or meters of copper cable, PCIe reach can extend to tens or even hundreds of meters. This capability enables new architectures built around resource disaggregation, accelerator pooling, memory expansion, and rack-scale AI infrastructure.</p>
<p>Ultimately, PCIe retimer reach is not determined by a single specification number. It is the cumulative result of SerDes excellence, intelligent controller design, comprehensive observability, high-quality channel engineering, and an appropriate transmission medium. The highest-performing solutions do more than satisfy PCI-SIG requirements. They provide the additional margin, interoperability, diagnostics, and robustness needed to maximize reach in the demanding AI, networking, storage, and data center environments of the future.</p>
<h3>Related link</h3>

		<title>Strengthening Advanced-Node Interconnects Through Automated Via Insertion</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/strengthening-advanced-node-interconnects-through-automated-via-insertion/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/strengthening-advanced-node-interconnects-through-automated-via-insertion/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Shehab Ashraf]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 15 Oct 2026 07:06:02 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Best Of Both: LP & HP]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Blogs - LPHP]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Low Power-High Performance]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[electromigration]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[interconnects]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[IR drop]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[physical design]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Short-resilient via insertion improves reliability and performance.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/strengthening-advanced-node-interconnects-through-automated-via-insertion/">Strengthening Advanced-Node Interconnects Through Automated Via Insertion</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>As the semiconductor industry pushes deeper into the sub-5nm realm, the physical design landscape has shifted from being dominated by gate delays to being defined by interconnect performance. In modern system-on-chip (SoC) designs, the wiring that connects billions of transistors has become the primary bottleneck for power, performance, and area (PPA). Among the various components of the interconnect stack, vias – the vertical connections between metal layers – represent one of the most significant points of vulnerability.</p>
<p>At advanced process nodes, via resistance increases exponentially as dimensions shrink. This rising resistance, coupled with higher current densities, exacerbates challenges related to electromigration (EM) and IR drop. Traditionally, design teams addressed these issues during the final signoff phase, often resulting in late-stage engineering change orders (ECOs) that could delay a project by weeks. To maintain aggressive time-to-market schedules while ensuring long-term silicon reliability, a new approach is required: shifting signoff-aware interconnect optimization into the implementation phase.</p>
<h2>The physics of via failure and interconnect resistance</h2>
<p>To understand the need for automated via optimization, first consider the physical challenges at play. In a typical advanced-node interconnect, the resistance of a single via can be significantly higher than that of a corresponding length of metal wire. As current flows through these narrow vertical structures, the resulting heat and atomic displacement can lead to electromigration – the gradual movement of metal atoms that eventually creates voids or shorts.</p>
<p>Plus, the cumulative effect of via resistance across a massive power delivery network (PDN) leads to IR drop. If the voltage reaching a logic gate falls below a certain threshold, the gate’s switching speed slows down, potentially leading to timing failures. In the worst cases, the gate may fail to switch entirely.</p>
<p>Historically, designers mitigated these risks by manually adding redundant vias to critical signal paths and power grids. The redundant vias provide parallel paths for current, lowering the effective resistance and reducing the current density through any single via. However, at 5nm and below, the sheer density of the layout and the complexity of foundry design rules make manual insertion practically impossible. Figure 1 illustrates the problem.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async" class="alignnone wp-image-24282822 size-full" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Siemens_Auto-Via-Insertion-fig1-dense-layout.jpg?resize=1748%2C1137&#038;ssl=1" alt="A high-density layout view showing the intricate metal and via layers of an advanced-node design, highlighting the limited space available for enhancement. Source: Siemens." width="1748" height="1137" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Siemens_Auto-Via-Insertion-fig1-dense-layout.jpg?w=1748&amp;ssl=1 1748w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Siemens_Auto-Via-Insertion-fig1-dense-layout.jpg?resize=300%2C195&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Siemens_Auto-Via-Insertion-fig1-dense-layout.jpg?resize=1024%2C666&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Siemens_Auto-Via-Insertion-fig1-dense-layout.jpg?resize=768%2C500&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Siemens_Auto-Via-Insertion-fig1-dense-layout.jpg?resize=1536%2C999&amp;ssl=1 1536w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Siemens_Auto-Via-Insertion-fig1-dense-layout.jpg?resize=600%2C390&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 1: The increasing complexity of advanced-node layouts requires automated solutions to identify valid locations for redundant via insertion without violating foundry rules. </strong></p>
<h2>The limitations of traditional implementation flows</h2>
<p>Most place-and-route (P&amp;R) tools include basic capabilities for via redundancy. However, these routers are primarily optimized for connectivity and timing closure, not for the exhaustive reliability enhancement required for high-performance silicon. Router-based via insertion typically comes with several limitations:</p>
<ol>
<li><strong>Lack of signoff awareness:</strong> Implementation routers typically use simplified versions of foundry design rules to maintain performance. While this is sufficient for initial routing, it often leads to DRC violations when the design is subjected to the full signoff rule deck.</li>
<li><strong>Limited search space:</strong> Routers often give up on via insertion in congested areas to avoid creating shorts. This leaves critical parts of the design – often the very areas that need the most help – under-optimized.</li>
<li><strong>ECO overhead:</strong> When a router-based enhancement triggers a signoff violation, the resulting ECO cycle requires re-running parts of the implementation flow, which consumes valuable time and can disrupt timing closure.</li>
</ol>
<p>To overcome these hurdles, many design teams adopt a &#8220;shift-left&#8221; methodology that uses signoff-quality engines earlier in the design cycle. By integrating the same logic used for final verification into the enhancement process, designers can achieve &#8220;correct-by-construction&#8221; results that are guaranteed to pass final signoff.</p>
<h2>Methodology: Automated signoff-aware enhancement</h2>
<p>The shift-left approach to via optimization involves a specialized enhancement platform that operates on the design database during the implementation phase. This platform reads standard design formats – such as LEF/DEF or OASIS – and applies a multi-step process to strengthen the interconnect.</p>
<p>The first step is a comprehensive analysis of the existing layout to identify every potential location where a redundant via could be placed. This is not a simple proximity check; the tool must account for complex multi-patterning constraints, voltage-aware spacing rules, and enclosure requirements. By leveraging a signoff-grade geometry engine, the tool can navigate these constraints with a level of precision that far exceeds traditional routers.</p>
<p>Once the valid insertion points are identified, the tool strategically adds redundant vias to the user-selected nets. This can be applied globally to the entire power grid or targeted toward specific high-priority signal nets, such as clock trees or long-distance bus lines. The result is a layout that is significantly more robust, with lower overall resistance and improved EM margins.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" class="alignnone wp-image-24282823 size-full" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Siemens_Auto-Via-Insertion-fig2-shift-left-de-via-methodology.jpg?resize=835%2C466&#038;ssl=1" alt="Diagram comparing a traditional linear signoff flow with the Calibre DesignEnhancer flow. The traditional flow, via insertion and EMIR analysis occur late. The &quot;Shift-left&quot; methodology, performs via insertion earlier, before signoff circuit (LVS) verification. Credit: Siemens." width="835" height="466" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Siemens_Auto-Via-Insertion-fig2-shift-left-de-via-methodology.jpg?w=835&amp;ssl=1 835w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Siemens_Auto-Via-Insertion-fig2-shift-left-de-via-methodology.jpg?resize=300%2C167&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Siemens_Auto-Via-Insertion-fig2-shift-left-de-via-methodology.jpg?resize=768%2C429&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Siemens_Auto-Via-Insertion-fig2-shift-left-de-via-methodology.jpg?resize=600%2C335&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 835px) 100vw, 835px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 2: By moving signoff-aware optimization into the implementation phase, design teams can resolve interconnect issues before they become late-stage bottlenecks. </strong></p>
<h2>Navigating layout imperfections with short-resilience</h2>
<p>One of the most innovative aspects of modern automated enhancement is the ability to handle &#8220;dirty&#8221; or incomplete layout data. A typical design database is rarely perfectly clean during the implementation flow. Localized shorts, routing overlaps, or incomplete power grid definitions are common as the design matures.</p>
<p>Traditional optimization tools often fail when encountering these imperfections, either crashing or producing illegal layout modifications. A robust enhancement platform must be &#8220;short-resilient.&#8221; This means the tool can identify regions with existing connectivity conflicts and automatically designate them as keep-out areas (Figure 3).</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282824" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Siemens_Auto-Via-Insertion-fig3-short-resiliant-flow.jpg?resize=821%2C255&#038;ssl=1" alt="A three part flowchart showing the process of avoiding via insertion on short-prone areas. 1-Early detection: analysis of LEF/DEF files to detect existing shorts. 2-Isolating shorts: A layout diagram shows a vertical metal line intersecting two horizontal metal lines; the intersection with a detected short is highlighted in red to isolate it. 3-DE Via run: The Calibre DesignEnhancer (DE) Via run, where a new via (highlighted in green) is successfully inserted on a clean intersection, while the tool avoids placing a via on the previously identified red short-prone region. Credit: Siemens" width="821" height="255" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Siemens_Auto-Via-Insertion-fig3-short-resiliant-flow.jpg?w=821&amp;ssl=1 821w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Siemens_Auto-Via-Insertion-fig3-short-resiliant-flow.jpg?resize=300%2C93&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Siemens_Auto-Via-Insertion-fig3-short-resiliant-flow.jpg?resize=768%2C239&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Siemens_Auto-Via-Insertion-fig3-short-resiliant-flow.jpg?resize=600%2C186&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 821px) 100vw, 821px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 3: Short-resilient DE-Via flow; avoiding insertion on identified short-prone regions.</strong></p>
<p>By protecting these suspicious regions, the tool can continue to optimize the rest of the design. This lets design teams run via enhancement early and often, even before the layout is fully DRC-clean. This iterative approach is essential for maintaining productivity in a fast-paced design environment, as it prevents minor layout issues from stalling the overall reliability enhancement of the chip.</p>
<h2>Impact on power delivery and electromigration</h2>
<p>The technical benefits of automated via insertion are most evident in the power delivery network. In high-performance SoCs, the PDN must deliver massive amounts of current with minimal voltage drop. As the number of metal layers increases, the vertical resistance through the via stacks becomes a dominant contributor to the total IR drop.</p>
<p>By maximizing the number of vias in the PDN, automated enhancement significantly lowers the vertical impedance of the grid. This leads to a more uniform voltage distribution across the die, providing more timing margin for the logic gates. In many cases, this enhancement can be the difference between meeting a performance target and having to down-clock the final product.</p>
<p>From an EM perspective, additional vias provide a critical safety net. Electromigration is a statistical phenomenon; while a single via might be designed to handle a specific current, manufacturing variations can lead to localized &#8220;hot spots&#8221; where the current density exceeds the safe limit. By providing parallel paths, automated insertion ensures that the current is distributed more evenly, reducing the likelihood of a catastrophic failure over the lifetime of the device.</p>
<h2>Scalability and integration in modern SoC flows</h2>
<p>As SoC designs grow to include billions of transistors and tens of kilometers of wiring, the scalability of the enhancement platform becomes vital. The tool must be able to process massive data volumes quickly enough to fit within a standard overnight implementation run. This requires a highly parallelized architecture that can distribute the layout analysis and insertion tasks across hundreds of CPU cores.</p>
<p>Furthermore, the platform must integrate seamlessly into the existing EDA ecosystem. By supporting standard industry formats and providing clear reporting on the enhancements made, the tool allows designers to maintain full control over their layouts. The ability to run &#8220;what-if&#8221; scenarios – such as testing the impact of different via densities on IR drop – provides designers with the insights needed to make informed trade-offs between PPA and reliability.</p>
<h2>Conclusion: The future of design robustness</h2>
<p>In the advanced-node era, the distinction between implementation and verification is blurring. The challenges of 5nm, 3nm, and beyond require that signoff awareness be present at every stage of the design cycle. Automated via insertion is a prime example of how this shift-left methodology can provide tangible benefits in terms of silicon reliability and schedule predictability.</p>
<p>By automating a traditionally manual and error-prone process, design teams can focus their efforts on higher-level architectural innovations, secure in the knowledge that their interconnects are built on a foundation of signoff-verified robustness. As interconnect challenges continue to mount, the adoption of automated, signoff-aware enhancement platforms will become not just an advantage, but a necessity for any team aiming to deliver high-performance silicon in the modern era.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/strengthening-advanced-node-interconnects-through-automated-via-insertion/">Strengthening Advanced-Node Interconnects Through Automated Via Insertion</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

		<title>Building AI Infrastructure For Greater Choice And Flexibility</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/building-ai-infrastructure-for-greater-choice-and-flexibility/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/building-ai-infrastructure-for-greater-choice-and-flexibility/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Mayank Bhatnagar]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 15 Oct 2026 07:03:05 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Blogs - LPHP]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Everything Low Power]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Low Power-High Performance]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[AI infrastructure]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Cadence]]></category>

		<category><![CDATA[open standards]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[training]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24282812</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Open interfaces and interoperability allow designers to choose technologies based on the needs of the system.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/building-ai-infrastructure-for-greater-choice-and-flexibility/">Building AI Infrastructure For Greater Choice And Flexibility</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>AI infrastructure is changing fast. Training and inference are putting different demands on compute, memory, connectivity, and networking, and there is no single architecture that fits every workload.</p>
<p>For system architects, this opens up an important question: How much flexibility can be built into the system from the start?</p>
<p>The answer increasingly involves giving designers more choices across memory, compute, connectivity, and packaging, while making sure those technologies work together.</p>
<h2>Different workloads, different requirements</h2>
<p>AI training and inference may run on much of the same underlying infrastructure, but they don&#8217;t behave the same way.</p>
<p>Training places heavy demands on memory and communication between accelerators. Inference has a different mix of requirements, including memory capacity, latency, throughput, and efficiency.</p>
<p>Those differences matter when choosing an architecture. A memory technology that&#8217;s right for one workload may not be right for another. The same applies to interconnects and networking.</p>
<p>This is why AI infrastructure is becoming more heterogeneous. Architects are combining different technologies based on what they need the system to do, rather than trying to force every workload into the same design.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282813" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Cadence_Building-AI-Infra-Choice-Flexibility-fig1.webp?resize=963%2C432&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="963" height="432" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Cadence_Building-AI-Infra-Choice-Flexibility-fig1.webp?w=963&amp;ssl=1 963w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Cadence_Building-AI-Infra-Choice-Flexibility-fig1.webp?resize=300%2C135&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Cadence_Building-AI-Infra-Choice-Flexibility-fig1.webp?resize=768%2C345&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Cadence_Building-AI-Infra-Choice-Flexibility-fig1.webp?resize=600%2C269&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 963px) 100vw, 963px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 1: Heterogeneous applications demand distinct solutions for optimized implementations.</strong></p>
<h2>More choice through open standards</h2>
<p>Open standards give designers more options for how they put those systems together.</p>
<p>UCIe is one example. The standard provides a common approach to die-to-die connectivity and is aimed at supporting an open chiplet ecosystem. It gives the industry a standardized way to connect dies within a package rather than tying the architecture to a single implementation.</p>
<p>System architects are also working across a wider range of process technologies, packaging approaches, and functions. A chiplet-based approach provides another way to partition those functions, allowing compute, I/O, memory interfaces, and other functions to be integrated within the same package.</p>
<p>UCIe provides a standardized die-to-die connection for that environment. This gives designers a common interface as they evaluate how different functions should be partitioned and integrated.</p>
<p>For designers, the value is choice. Different functions can be brought together in a package while using a common interface between them.</p>
<p>That freedom becomes particularly useful when architects are balancing performance, power, cost, packaging, and process technology.</p>
<h2>Interoperability matters</h2>
<p>Open standards provide a common foundation for bringing technologies from different suppliers and foundries into the same system. Interoperability helps designers understand how those different implementations will work together.</p>
<p>Verification plays an important role here, particularly as systems incorporate more functions, interfaces, and technologies.</p>
<h2>The same thinking applies across the AI factory</h2>
<p>The need for choice doesn&#8217;t stop at the package.</p>
<p>An AI system can include several kinds of connectivity, each serving a different role. PCIe, CXL, UCIe, UALink, and Ethernet-based technologies address different parts of the architecture. Memory brings another set of decisions.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282814" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Cadence_Building-AI-Infra-Choice-Flexibility-fig2.webp?resize=975%2C650&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="975" height="650" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Cadence_Building-AI-Infra-Choice-Flexibility-fig2.webp?w=975&amp;ssl=1 975w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Cadence_Building-AI-Infra-Choice-Flexibility-fig2.webp?resize=300%2C200&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Cadence_Building-AI-Infra-Choice-Flexibility-fig2.webp?resize=768%2C512&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Cadence_Building-AI-Infra-Choice-Flexibility-fig2.webp?resize=600%2C400&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 975px) 100vw, 975px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 2: Different connectivity, different scope, same goal: economical, rapid data transfer.</strong></p>
<p>The requirements also change depending on where data is moving. HBM4E and LPDDR6 address different memory needs, while PCIe supports high-speed host and device connectivity. UALink addresses accelerator-to-accelerator communication, 224G high-speed SerDes provides the underlying high-speed signaling needed for demanding connectivity applications, and UCIe connects dies within packages.</p>
<p>Designers need to consider what they are connecting, how much data needs to move, and the requirements of the workload. Looking at those decisions together provides a more complete view of the system than treating each interface independently.</p>
<p>That perspective changes the design conversation. Rather than optimizing individual pieces independently, architects can look at how memory, compute, and connectivity fit together across the system.</p>
<h2>Designing with room to evolve</h2>
<p>AI infrastructure will continue to change as workloads, memory technologies, accelerators, and interconnects advance. Building flexibility into the architecture gives designers more options as those requirements change.</p>
<p>Open interfaces and interoperability are an important part of that flexibility, allowing designers to choose technologies based on the needs of the system rather than a single approach.</p>
<p>For a deeper look at the memory, compute, and connectivity technologies shaping these systems, read our <a href="https://www.cadence.com/content/dam/cadence-www/global/en_US/documents/tools/silicon-solutions/building-ai-factories-with-ip-solutions-wp.pdf">Building AI Factories with IP Solutions white paper</a>.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/building-ai-infrastructure-for-greater-choice-and-flexibility/">Building AI Infrastructure For Greater Choice And Flexibility</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

		<title>AMBA C2C: Moving Forward With A Converged AMBA Foundation For C2C Connectivity</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/amba-c2c-moving-forward-with-a-converged-amba-foundation-for-c2c-connectivity/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/amba-c2c-moving-forward-with-a-converged-amba-foundation-for-c2c-connectivity/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Francisco Socal]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 15 Oct 2026 07:02:37 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[At The Core]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Blogs - LPHP]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Low Power-High Performance]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[AMBA]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[AMBA C2C]]></category>

		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24282807</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Extending chiplet connectivity across AXI and CHI with scalable protocol subsets, interoperability, and flexible transport support.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/amba-c2c-moving-forward-with-a-converged-amba-foundation-for-c2c-connectivity/">AMBA C2C: Moving Forward With A Converged AMBA Foundation For C2C Connectivity</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>In this blog post, we introduce AMBA C2C, a new specification being developed with the AMBA ecosystem. It provides a unified and scalable approach to connecting AMBA protocols across chiplets, including AMBA AXI and AMBA CHI.</p>
<h2>The evolving C2C landscape</h2>
<p>Chiplet technology and AI are evolving rapidly, bringing new benefits and protocol requirements.</p>
<p><a href="https://newsroom.arm.com/blog/amba-chi-c2c-specification">AMBA CHI C2C has established strong momentum as a foundational protocol for chiplets and chip-to-chip (C2C)</a> connectivity. It is particularly suited to fully coherent, advanced heterogeneous compute and superchips.</p>
<p>However, chiplets span a much wider range of use cases. These include memory expansion, IO and accelerator attach, and advanced heterogeneous systems. Each use case comes with different requirements and trade-offs in functionality, performance, bandwidth efficiency, and implementation complexity.</p>
<p>AMBA CHI C2C already supports <a href="https://support.arm.com/documentation/112071/0100/">scalability in implementation complexity through a property negotiation mechanism</a>. Implementations can support only the capabilities they need while preserving interoperability across chiplet types, vendors, and generations.</p>
<p>Our continued collaboration with the ecosystem has highlighted an important additional requirement. Many chiplets do not need the full feature set of advanced coherent systems and require an even simpler approach for C2C connectivity. This is particularly important for the vast installed base of AXI-based designs. These designs can benefit from the greater reuse and composability that chiplets enable.</p>
<p>This has been an important focus area since <a href="https://developer.arm.com/community/arm-community-blogs/b/servers-and-cloud-computing-blog/posts/multi-chip-and-chi-c2c">we first introduced AMBA CHI C2C in 2023</a>. At that time, we discussed how C2C connectivity could extend to simpler, often AXI-based use cases. Partner feedback since then has reinforced the need for a unified and converged C2C approach for AMBA protocols. This approach includes both CHI and AXI, rather than separate, protocol-specific point solutions.</p>
<h2>Introducing AMBA C2C</h2>
<p>To address these evolving requirements, we are developing AMBA C2C.</p>
<p>AMBA C2C builds on the success of AMBA CHI C2C. It provides a converged and scalable C2C foundation across AMBA protocols, including AXI and CHI.</p>
<p>At the heart of AMBA C2C is protocol subsetting. Defined subsets enable the protocol feature set and complexity to scale across different use cases. For example, device or accelerator attach subsets can support the simpler requirements aligned with AXI-based IO and non-coherent traffic. More advanced subsets can support the richer functionality required by coherent and heterogeneous systems.</p>
<p>AMBA C2C uses defined protocol subsets to scale functionality and implementation complexity across different use cases. These subsets can align with on-chip protocols such as AXI and CHI. AMBA C2C then defines how these protocols are packetized for chip-to-chip transport. The packetization is optimized for each subset while providing a common approach across AXI- and CHI-class traffic.</p>
<p>Interoperability remains fundamental to the architecture. AMBA C2C builds on the property negotiation mechanism introduced with AMBA CHI C2C. This mechanism enables implementations with different capabilities to interoperate across chiplet types, vendors, and generations. This includes backwards and forwards compatibility.</p>
<h2>A layered architecture for an evolving industry</h2>
<p>An open chiplet ecosystem requires open standards and a clear, layered standardization approach. This includes a clear separation between the protocol and the underlying transport.</p>
<p>This is a proven industry model that UCIe and the broader ecosystem have adopted. AMBA CHI C2C, for example, uses UCIe Streaming as <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OtA8m1AVOTw&amp;t=2386s">discussed</a> in the <a href="https://www.uciexpress.org/post/ucie-1-1-provides-streaming-protocol-solution-for-error-detection-and-replay">UCIe 1.1 specification announcement</a>.</p>
<p>Similarly, PCIe and CXL protocols can be transported over UCIe. More recently, UALink has adopted a similar layered architecture. It defines a packetization strategy alongside its protocol functionality while separating it from the underlying data-link and physical layers.</p>
<p>AMBA C2C follows this same principle. AMBA defines the protocol and packetization mechanism, while transports such as UCIe provide the underlying die-to-die connectivity. This enables AMBA C2C to work with a variety of die-to-die and chip-to-chip transports. More importantly, it provides a clean architectural boundary that enables AMBA protocols and underlying transport technologies to continue evolving at pace.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282808" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Arm_AMBA-C2C-converged-foundation-fig1.png?resize=1682%2C520&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1682" height="520" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Arm_AMBA-C2C-converged-foundation-fig1.png?w=1682&amp;ssl=1 1682w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Arm_AMBA-C2C-converged-foundation-fig1.png?resize=300%2C93&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Arm_AMBA-C2C-converged-foundation-fig1.png?resize=1024%2C317&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Arm_AMBA-C2C-converged-foundation-fig1.png?resize=768%2C237&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Arm_AMBA-C2C-converged-foundation-fig1.png?resize=1536%2C475&amp;ssl=1 1536w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Arm_AMBA-C2C-converged-foundation-fig1.png?resize=600%2C185&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 1: Transporting AMBA protocols over UCIe with AMBA C2C.</strong></p>
<p>For AMBA AXI, this separation is particularly important. AXI is widely adopted across the industry and continues to evolve. However, unlike packet-based protocols, AXI defines interface behavior rather than a native packet format. AXI is also highly configurable, and capabilities vary between implementations. Transporting AXI over a C2C link therefore requires an architectural definition. This definition specifies which AXI semantics are carried and how they are packetized. That definition must evolve alongside AXI itself.</p>
<h2>Putting it all together</h2>
<p>AMBA C2C is the next evolution of AMBA’s C2C work. It builds on AMBA CHI C2C and extends the approach to a broader range of AMBA-based chiplet systems.</p>
<p>AMBA C2C provides a common foundation that can scale from simple AXI-based designs to advanced, CHI-based fully coherent heterogeneous systems. Interoperability is built into the architecture.</p>
<p>AMBA C2C follows the development and licensing model that has supported the AMBA ecosystem for decades. We are developing it in collaboration with industry partners. The specification will be freely available, royalty-free, and architecture-neutral. Over decades, this model has helped establish AMBA as a dependable and trusted industry foundation. It has supported widespread adoption, a thriving ecosystem, and a broad marketplace of compatible solutions.</p>
<p>We look forward to continuing our collaboration with the industry to enable an open, interoperable chiplet ecosystem, with AMBA C2C evolving alongside complementary industry standards.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/amba-c2c-moving-forward-with-a-converged-amba-foundation-for-c2c-connectivity/">AMBA C2C: Moving Forward With A Converged AMBA Foundation For C2C Connectivity</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

		<item>
		<title>Why Open-Weight AI Matters</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/why-open-weight-ai-matters/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/why-open-weight-ai-matters/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Ann Mutschler]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 15 Oct 2026 07:02:13 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Low Power-High Performance]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Top Stories]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[AI]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Arteris]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Axiomise]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Ayar Labs]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Cadence]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[ChipAgents]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Expedera]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Movellus]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[open-weight AI models]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Quadric]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Rambus]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Siemens EDA]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Synopsys]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24282836</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Proprietary models still hold the edge, but open-weight models add more flexibility for deploying AI.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/why-open-weight-ai-matters/">Why Open-Weight AI Matters</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p><strong>Key Takeaways:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Local inference and model routing can help manage cost and protect sensitive data, but chip architects must account for memory capacity, sustained performance, changing models, and deployment security.</li>
<li>For EDA, model quality depends on clean, trusted design data and integration into workflows, not just on choosing a larger model or fine-tuning its weights.</li>
<li>Open weights can reduce dependence on proprietary AI services, but they do not automatically provide open training data, source code, or unrestricted usage rights.</li>
</ul>
<hr />
<p>Open-weight AI models are creating new challenges for chip architects as rapidly changing workloads strain memory, interconnects, and compute flexibility.</p>
<p>The focus is no longer just peak TOPS. The checklist has grown to include the best way to feed memory-hungry models, sustain performance across long-context and multi-agent inference, support rapidly changing numeric formats and sparse computation, and isolate models, data, and tools as part of the security boundary. Model architectures can change in weeks while silicon takes years, so the winners will build adaptable hardware-software platforms, rather than accelerators optimized for a benchmark that may be obsolete before tape-out.</p>
<p>Massive data centers are not a prerequisite for AI-driven scientific advances. Science has different infrastructure needs from consumer AI platforms serving millions of users. Open-weight AI models — whose trained parameters are publicly available — can be deployed locally, potentially widening access, improving compute efficiency, and supporting independent research.</p>
<p>Open weights also raise questions about control, cost, and who can build on AI technology.</p>
<p>Sharad Chole, chief scientist and co-founder at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/expedera/">Expedera</a>, said publishing weights can reduce vendor lock-in as it allows users to host a model themselves or choose a service provider. “If you want to use a service, or host it yourself, there is no vendor lock-in in terms of who is providing the next token for you or who is servicing your next request. But there are geopolitical and investment sides to it. There is also a push for open hardware, like what Meta and others do to enable different competing solution providers. As of September 2026, the larger open-weight models come primarily from outside the U.S., either Europe or Asia, and we are moving toward trillion-parameter models.”</p>
<p>Open-weight models make trained parameters downloadable, letting users run and adapt them on their own hardware rather than relying on a provider’s API, according to Guillaume Boillet, vice president of strategic marketing at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/arterisip/">Arteris</a>. “They are not necessarily open source: training data, code and usage rights may remain restricted.”</p>
<p>While open-weight AI model releases publish trained parameters, open-source releases aim to publish the full recipe, and closed models publish neither, said Ashish Darbari, CEO of <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/axiomise/">Axiomise</a>.</p>
<p>Representative open-weight releases include Meta Llama, Alibaba Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, Google Gemma, Microsoft Phi, and OpenAI’s gpt-oss family. OpenAI reports that gpt-oss-120b runs on a single 80 GB GPU and gpt-oss-20b can run on devices with 16 GB of memory; both use MXFP4 quantization, Darbari noted. “These specifications illustrate the widening range of deployment options, but memory fit alone does not establish useful performance.&#8221;</p>
<p>Some U.S.-based AI companies use knowledge distillation to develop smaller models from larger teacher models, but approaches vary. Smaller models may also be pretrained independently or developed through a mix of techniques. Large-scale pretraining remains computationally intensive, while distillation and post-training are important parts of the model-development process.</p>
<p>Chole said the largest models continue to push toward trillion-parameter scales, while models intended for devices or local AI are often distilled into smaller versions. “It’s not like suddenly we’re going to have 100-billion-parameter models breaking all the benchmark records,” he said. He cited an effort to distill a 400-billion-parameter DeepSeek-C model into an 8-billion-parameter Qwen model, while noting that model distillation itself is not new. The broader point is that users now have many choices across model size, capability, and deployment method, and the largest model is not necessarily the right choice for every task.</p>
<p>On Hugging Face, the ‘GitHub for AI models’, there have been approximately 250 open-weight models released in the last two years by major companies, not including quantized variants or models from smaller companies, Chole noted.</p>
<p>But abundance is not the same as readiness, and turning this expanding model catalog into useful design intelligence requires EDA teams to supply trusted domain data, workflow context and rigorous ground truth.</p>
<p><strong>From general-purpose models to EDA workflows</strong><br />
Whether commercial or open-source, general-purpose LLMs aren&#8217;t built for chip design tasks, according to Thomas Andersen, vice president for AI and machine learning at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/synopsys-inc/">Synopsys</a>. “A lot of them are very good at common tasks. They&#8217;re very good at creating PowerPoints and summarizing things. They&#8217;re good at coding, obviously, because there&#8217;s a lot of code out there. Those have been optimized to death. They&#8217;re not necessarily well suited to hardware development, not even the RTL coding, because even the RTL that’s out there is just not nearly as much as software. Because of that, every party, including EDA vendors and customers, needs to add their data, and that data is obviously proprietary. This is the difference versus all these models that take public knowledge and put it into the training data. There are both pre- and post-training capabilities, even beyond the weights themselves, where you can add data, and that&#8217;s an important key point. Otherwise, it just doesn&#8217;t work. It&#8217;s like asking a chatbot a question. It doesn&#8217;t always give the right answer because it has conflicting data, searches the internet, and people say all kinds of things. What&#8217;s the ground truth?”</p>
<p>Accurate results rely on both the query and the quality of the source data.</p>
<p>“The source data itself needs to be very clear, very crisp,” Andersen said. “On the internet, it doesn&#8217;t exist. You go on Reddit, people will say five different things when you ask them a question. That becomes the problem of the LLM. In our case, we obviously need very crisp data. In a corporate environment, it&#8217;s different. You have much better documentation of processes, of tools, and so on, so it&#8217;s a little bit easier. Without that, it doesn&#8217;t work. Still, general training of run-of-the-mill models is absolutely required.”</p>
<p>That said, open-weight models will have a place in chip design. “An open-weight model simply means you have an LLM model where you can train the weights of the model,” Andersen explained. “Agentic is a loop that sits around this LLM and then does certain tasks, so it&#8217;s a means to an end. There are multiple ways to train the model, which is more like tuning the answer&#8217;s correctness, but it doesn&#8217;t actually add data itself. There are other ways to add data. Once you have, let&#8217;s say, an LLM that knows everything the way you as a human would, then agentic just means you’re building an agentic loop that essentially optimizes your workflow, that does a sequence of tasks the way you as a human would do, rather than one-shot things. Or, you just ask a question and it comes back.”</p>
<p>That distinction between the model and the workflow around it leads directly to a practical deployment question: How should EDA teams route each task to the right model while balancing capability, cost, and control?</p>
<p>Ankur Gupta, executive vice president and head of EDA IC software at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/mentor-a-siemens-business/">Siemens EDA</a>, noted that anyone who is super cost-conscious, from a big chip design company to a small one, still wants to optimize. “They want to pay for the best commercial model, as long as it fits the task, so key architects can solve the hardest problems. It&#8217;s called model routing. We know that open-weight models are very useful. They&#8217;re effective. EDA companies are playing with them. We certainly are. Many of our developers are using open-weight models extensively because you don&#8217;t need to go pay a bunch of money for every single task. And I see this in our customers. They have pulled back on opening up the highest-strength models to everybody, and they&#8217;re doing model routing internally. We haven&#8217;t.&#8221;</p>
<p>Gupta suggests thinking about it in the context of an iceberg. “What you see above the water level is GPU and costs and tokens and all that. That&#8217;s on every CIO&#8217;s dashboard. It hasn&#8217;t gone away. What&#8217;s under the surface is also equally important. It&#8217;s connecting the silicon to the system to the facilities. There&#8217;s lossiness there that you have to recover cost from. Somebody&#8217;s going to figure out how to make token cost very viable, just like the entire semiconductor industry has been operating that way, like building in functionality and making that functionality cheaper. It&#8217;s just a matter of time before that happens.”</p>
<p>Steven Woo, fellow and distinguished inventor at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/rambus-inc/">Rambus</a>, sees open-weight AI models as very helpful to chip designers. “You look at the success stories from companies like OpenAI with the Jalapeno chip and using their own tools, having a smaller team that was both nimbler and more able to do more turns more quickly. Designing that chip in nine months and getting it to work the first time out was incredible. We know that work has been going on in this area, and the tools are just getting better.”</p>
<p>The caveat is that organizations need to maintain control of data that distinguishes them from competitors. “In the beginning, when you had to access these things on the web, there weren&#8217;t private, walled areas where a company could ensure its data stayed inside, and many companies were reluctant to let employees use the technology,&#8221; Woo said. &#8220;But the industry heard and said, ‘Okay, well now we&#8217;re going to set up walled areas where we can be certain that your information won&#8217;t leak.’ The general idea of how to design a chip — for example, writing RTL to do certain functions and doing place-and-route — there are many examples out there that you can use to train a large language model or an AI entity to do this. Different industries and different companies have very specific ways they approach solutions to problems. Those you can&#8217;t really let out because they&#8217;re more like trade secrets. So then the question is, &#8216;How do I take these models that are trained on more general sets and tune them — really fine-tune them — to the specifics of what I do and what my customers care about, and that can&#8217;t leave the walled area?&#8217; I&#8217;m hopeful that that kind of thing gets solved.”</p>
<p>Open-weight AI models might also be useful in the EDA tool flow to help control costs. “Cost is a big deal, and we want our customers to pay us, not the AI vendors,&#8221; said Chuck Alpert, AI fellow at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/cadence-design-systems/">Cadence</a>. &#8220;The idea is that open-weight models are going to help keep the costs under control for customers. How do we do that? If you have an open-weight model, you can put it on a machine and never leave your network. If you&#8217;re using, say, Claude Opus [a closed, proprietary model by Anthropic], you have to leave the network. Some customers — maybe defense customers especially, who are very sensitive about their information — are part of an ecosystem that says they want to use agentic AI but don&#8217;t want to leave their system. A customer like that has to use Openlayer [an enterprise AI evaluation, observability, and governance platform]. There’s also currently the issue that open-weight models may not perform well. They&#8217;re getting better, and I&#8217;m finding some of them are quite good. But they&#8217;re still lagging, which is where doing some training of open-weight models could be a real improvement and an important development, and that we&#8217;re actively pursuing.”</p>
<p>One of the keys here is clearly defining the problem statement. &#8220;If you think about what chip design is, there&#8217;s a massive, multi-physics component, and then you distill it down to a math model, which is extensive — it could be 100,000 lines of the transistor model,&#8221; said Mo Faisal, CEO of <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/movellus/">Movellus</a>. &#8220;After that, it is just matrix multiplication. When and how, I&#8217;m not sure, but it probably will be one of the new startups that is building semiconductor-specific models. They may start opening up the older things that are maybe trained on 180nm, and you can go build a chip of that and not open up whatever works with the more advanced nodes or more advanced architectures. There&#8217;s probably a surprise coming from the Googles or Microsofts or Metas of the world. Why can&#8217;t they open-weight their silicon models, since they do have internal silicon design models that they use?”</p>
<p>That possibility shifts the discussion from whether open-weight models can serve EDA to how their business model shapes where — and on what hardware — those models are deployed.</p>
<p><strong>Distinguishing features</strong><br />
Open- and closed-weight models can use similar underlying architectures.</p>
<p>“The architectures are the same — the same transformer blocks, the same attention mechanisms, the same quantization tricks,&#8221; said Steve Roddy, chief marketing officer at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/quadric/">Quadric</a>. &#8220;A chip architect looking at the two would not be able to tell them apart from the compute graph. The difference is entirely a business model distinction. One vendor publishes the parameters for download, the other sells access by the token.&#8221;</p>
<p>That difference is what drives deployment. “In practice, the small and mid-sized open-weight models are the ones technically sophisticated users — engineers mostly — download and run on their own hardware, and the motivation is overwhelmingly cost,” Roddy said. “Some run locally to keep prompt data private, and that matters in regulated industries, but token economics is by far the bigger driver today.”</p>
<p>Roddy expects the closed-model vendors to come after that local token volume. “It would surprise no one to see the large private model companies orchestrate split deployments — a midsize front-end model running on the user&#8217;s own hardware, with the large model in the cloud handling what the local model can&#8217;t. Those big model companies absolutely do not want some other vendor or other model running locally to become the front door that gates access to the big paid model in the cloud. The pricing incentive is obvious — offer dramatically cheaper (maybe free) tokens for the ones the user generates on their own machine, on their own electricity, and cut the data center rental bill enormously. When an offhand tweet (Sam Altman, April 2025) says that the cost of users typing &#8216;thank you&#8217; runs to tens of millions of dollars, the pressure to offload inference to the edge is not subtle.”</p>
<p>All of that puts pressure on local machines to run larger models, or portions of those models that are disaggregated into smaller models. “The world cannot build data centers fast enough, and it is not going to. But we can plug something the size of a household appliance into every home and office,” Roddy said. “That opens a new category of compute — the agentic computer, architected around running AI models as its primary workload, not as an afterthought bolted onto a phone or PC designed for something else. Today&#8217;s devices treat inference as a guest. The next generation will treat it as the host. The question chip architects should be asking is not, ‘How do I add an NPU to my SoC?’ It&#8217;s, ‘What does a system look like when model execution is the main job?’ Memory bandwidth and capacity, not TOPS. Sustained throughput, not burst benchmarks. Thermal envelope for continuous rather than intermittent load. And a software stack that can absorb a new model architecture every few months without a silicon respin.”</p>
<p>One of the problems here is the mismatch between chip and model cycles. “If you&#8217;re designing a chip for a particular model, models are changing on a weekly basis, or at best monthly, and your chip design cycle is in the best-case scenario 2.5 years,&#8221; said Vishal Chandrasekar, director of product management at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/ayar-labs/">Ayar Labs</a>. &#8220;So how you are intercepting something over that kind of a time frame is hard to see. At the same time, chips that were made in 2019 are still valuable today, because now maybe you&#8217;re compute-limited. So a model that&#8217;s released today, even if there are 10 new models in two years, is still useful for some application.&#8221;</p>
<p>That mismatch makes adaptability the central design requirement — and it frames the practical questions chip architects must answer before committing to an open-weight AI platform.</p>
<p>Solaiman Rahim, chief product officer at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/alpha-design-ai-chipagents/">ChipAgents</a><strong>,</strong> said chip designers should understand that the weights are open, so anyone can use them. “Not only the weights, but also the task list and the dataset they were trained on are provided with the model. So, if anybody wants to rebuild the model, they can. The goal of open-weight models is to give you a base model you can fine-tune to your needs, and performance and cost vary depending on the model. People think open-weight models perform poorly and cost little, but that&#8217;s not true. If you look at the latest open-weight model, GLM 5.3, the performance is pretty good. It&#8217;s in the 70% to 80% range, but the cost is also very high. It&#8217;s not because it&#8217;s open-weight that you necessarily get the lowest performance and the lowest cost. The cost and performance of many open-weight models really depend on which model you&#8217;re using. But it&#8217;s a good base model to fine-tune and build your workflow on top of to get your desired outcome. You also need to figure out how to integrate an open-weight model into your infrastructure.”</p>
<p>Deployment may be on-premises or in a cloud environment such as a virtual private cloud, depending on security requirements and whether a company is comfortable sharing data with its provider. “If you go to AWS, their cloud is very secure. Many customers use VPCs in AWS or other cloud providers, so you need to decide how you want to deploy that model,” Rahim said. “The model alone isn&#8217;t enough to start a cost-effective design task. You need to build the ontology layer yourself. You have to build the workflows. Our platform does that automatically so you don&#8217;t spend your time and investment trying to reinvent the same way that EDA was built 30 years ago. When everyone did their own synthesis, they came up with Design Compiler, which showed them they could do it with one and didn&#8217;t need to reinvent everything. The same thing is happening right now. We have our ontology, our workflows, and our own model layer. Our model layer can pick the best model for you automatically based on the task.”</p>
<p>Other considerations the architecture and design team should ask about include defining the range of models the system must support rather than predicting a single future model size, said Arteris&#8217; Boillet. “Important variables include active parameter count, precision, context length, modality, concurrency, and latency. Teams should ask whether a smaller specialized model is sufficient, where the working set will reside, and how energy use changes under realistic loads. The meaningful measure is energy per useful result, not just TOPS or TDP.”</p>
<p>Taken together, those workload variables turn model selection into a system-architecture problem, with direct consequences for memory, compute, interconnect, and verification.</p>
<p>Axiomise&#8217;s Darbari noted that if more inference moves out of hyperscale data centers, it could shift inference silicon toward institutional servers, workstations, laptops, and edge SoCs running 1 billion to 100 billion parameter mixture-of-experts models locally, with a number of architectural implications such as:</p>
<ol>
<li>Memory bandwidth, not FLOPS, as the binding constraint;</li>
<li>Sparse activation to change the arithmetic;</li>
<li>Low-precision in the ISA and datapath;</li>
<li>Heterogeneous SoCs as the delivery vehicle;</li>
<li>Mini-fridge servers as a real product category, and</li>
<li>Verification and PPA sign-off exercising MoE-style sparse traffic, MXFP4 arithmetic, KV-cache pressure at 128K context, and multi-agent concurrency, not just dense GEMM.</li>
</ol>
<p>Those architectural priorities become concrete when teams estimate what it takes not merely to fit a model in memory, but to run it responsively in daily engineering workflows.</p>
<p>“Capable language, vision-language, and reasoning models with 20 billion to 30 billion parameters can now fit in roughly 16 to 24 GiB of memory after quantization,” Boillet said. “In my own synthetic benchmark on a 36 GB MacBook, models in this range fit. But fitting in memory was not the same as running productively. For the responsiveness needed to replace cloud models in daily work and agentic workflows, the cost can still climb above $10,000. Chip architects need to size compute, memory, and interconnect for the intended application while leaving room for the model mix to change. Being open-weight does not change the underlying model arithmetic. It does let users change precision, sparsity, fine-tuning, and model structure, so memory bandwidth, data movement, numeric flexibility, and quality of service matter more than peak TOPS alone. A dense model and a mixture-of-experts model with the same total parameter count can load the system very differently. Security priorities include authenticating model files and updates, protecting memory and DMA paths, isolating workloads, and supporting rollback.”</p>
<p><strong>Conclusion</strong><br />
Open-weight AI will not eliminate the tradeoffs facing chip architects, but it will make them more explicit. Successful platforms will be designed around adaptable model mixes, sustained memory and interconnect performance, realistic energy and latency targets, and security that extends from authenticated weights through runtimes, tools, and data. For EDA teams, the advantage will come not from choosing open or closed models in isolation, but from combining the right models with trusted domain knowledge, disciplined routing, and hardware-software systems that can evolve long after tape-out.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/why-open-weight-ai-matters/">Why Open-Weight AI Matters</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
