					<description><![CDATA[<p>Agentic workloads increase CPU demand, while reasoning models, MoE architectures, and reservoir computing fuel AI acceleration.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/agentic-ai-alters-the-cpu-gpu-balance/">Agentic AI Alters The CPU-GPU Balance</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p><strong>Key Takeaways:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Agentic AI, reasoning models, mixture-of-expert architectures, and reservoir computing are changing how AI workloads use compute resources.</li>
<li>Agentic AI is particularly popular, and because it requires more CPU, CPU supply is coming under pressure.</li>
<li>Mixture-of-experts models are becoming very popular, enabling specialized queries that require fewer parameters to load.</li>
</ul>
<hr />
<p>Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and large language models (LLMs) have dominated commercial AI for some time. Proprietary recommender models for companies such as Meta have also had significant societal impact even though only one company employs each such model. GPUs perform the heavy lifting for many of those types of models. But agentic AI needs more orchestration, and that’s a job for CPUs.</p>
<p>When AI’s only job is to run a model, it turns to GPUs or dedicated neural processing units (NPUs). Agents still use these models, but each is only part of the solution. Those agents must make decisions based on what the models return, and that requires if-then-else logic, and that’s what CPUs are good at. GPUs, not so much. According to some industry estimates, agentic workloads could alter the ratio of CPUs to GPUs from 1:4 to as low as 1:1.</p>
<p>Newer model types are also emerging, most of which are still based on LLM fundamentals. Unlike agentic AI, reasoning models, mixture-of-expert (MoE) models, and reservoir computing still rely on GPUs. But they’re also ripe for use by agents.</p>
<p><strong>Pixels and parsing<br />
</strong>For several years, practical, commercial AI meant CNNs and recurrent neural networks, or RNNs. The former were good at analyzing camera input, while the latter were proficient at analyzing sound and language. The second “L” in LLM means “language,” but LLMs do much more than language today. The notion is that some piece of text is abstracted into a token, and now practically anything can be a token.</p>
<p>The benefit of LLMs over RNNs is that they can maintain an arbitrarily long context, making them better at picking the right words when interpreting and generating text. In addition to requiring fewer resources, RNNs can analyze incoming frames of sound immediately without waiting to establish context, improving real-time response.</p>
<p>The challenge with early LLMs was that they had one job — to predict a likely next word in a sequence. That word had to make sense syntactically, but not necessarily semantically, and it certainly didn’t check facts to ensure correctness, hence the frequent “hallucinations.”</p>
<p>One way to improve that was through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Instead of just figuring out a word that could maybe work, models could access “embeddings” that contained real facts, helping generate text that was both syntactically, semantically, and factually correct.</p>
<p><strong>Secret agent man<br />
</strong>Today’s hot topic is, of course, agentic AI. An agent is a new entity, not one that replaces or modifies an LLM (or any other model). It effectively represents a higher level of abstraction, acting as an orchestrator of models. It’s not a model itself, although it must be trained.</p>
<p>“There is some new research out there that says agentic inference is going to dwarf everything else put together before it,” said Ed Doe, CEO and co-founder of Delos Data.</p>
<p>The whole point of an agent is that it does more than find an answer to a question. It does something with that answer. What it does will likely depend on the answers it’s received so far. In other words, it can send tokens to a model and, when it receives the result, decide what to do next, embarking on a sequence of decisions and actions.</p>
<p>A well-trained agent is meant to handle a set of tasks without tight supervision. “If, as a leader, you have to tell your team every step to accomplish, you&#8217;re going to be more consumed with every step of the way,” explained Rob Knoth, product management director, digital and signoff group at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/cadence-design-systems/">Cadence</a>. “But if you say, ‘I need you to go over there and get this work done,’ then you can go focus on another task, occasionally looking over to make sure that things are going well.”</p>
<p>This is a new space. “Since last year, agentic AI took off,” noted Satadal Bhattacharjee, global head of cloud and AI infrastructure silicon at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/arm/">Arm</a>. “Now you can say, ‘I want to go to Costa Rica for 10 days. I need hotels, car rental, and entry tickets for these parks. Here is my budget. Go and reserve all of that.’ You give it an outline, just like to a travel agent, then the agent calls APIs to take action on your behalf.”</p>
<p><strong>A new job for CPUs<br />
</strong>An agent’s decisions typically involve if-then-else branching, and that’s not what GPUs are good at. CPUs do far better at such decision-heavy code, so they’re becoming a more important part of the computing cluster. For typical LLMs, they mainly serve as hosts, setting things up and managing communication through PCI for things like scale-out. That’s a relatively light CPU load, allowing it to handle host duties for multiple GPUs at the same time. The ratio of CPUs to GPUs will vary by system, but it’s around 1:4 for typical LLMs.</p>
<p>With agents, CPUs will be far busier doing actual work (rather than just enabling the GPUs to do work). So while the GPU has been the belle of the ball for a long time, CPUs are getting renewed respect as the CPU: GPU ratio moves closer to 1:1. That will also raise demand for CPUs, which can nudge prices upward.</p>
<p>“The challenge used to be how many AI accelerators we can get per CPU,” said Ron Lowman, strategic marketing manager for IP at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/synopsys-inc/">Synopsys</a>. “With agentic AI, there&#8217;s more CPU load demand, and therefore the ratios have changed.”</p>
<p>Bhattacharjee agreed. “Demand for CPU has risen a lot because everyone is looking for a lot more compute and in a power-efficient way to run these agents,” he said.</p>
<p>“In the last 18 months, everyone is clamoring over agentic AI,” said Yong Meng Sua, CTO at QCI. “This is why CPUs are getting very expensive right now.”</p>
<p>“The CPU is back, but is being used in a very different way than it was used in the rest of the data center,” Doe said.</p>
<p>Agentic queries are also more compute-intensive because, instead of just one query, sending a request to an agent typically results in many queries as the agent completes its series of tasks.</p>
<p>More advanced agents must also understand sequencing, and that can be programmed. “There is a programming part as well,” Arm’s Bhattacharjee said. “You can run JSON scripts to tune it and sequence it. There&#8217;s a lot more that can be done with agents.”</p>
<p><strong>Show your work<br />
</strong>The other challenge with early models is that humans can’t understand them. Models are a big cloud of numbers, and no single number can realistically be tied to anything physical or factual. The weights achieved during training aren’t sacrosanct. Training starts with random weights that get refined over many passes. Start with a different random assignment and the training will evolve to a different — and yet still correct — model.</p>
<p>So how do you prove that your solution is correct even if it is one of many possible correct models? There’s no deterministic way to trace how a basic model performs its calculations, making it hard to certify systems that must, for example, be safe. And the notion of safety is expanding as frontier models behave badly and escape their sandboxes, for example.</p>
<p>Reasoning models use additional inferencing before generating answers to queries, and in some cases they provide an accounting of how they arrived at an answer. “Reasoning is where it uses its knowledge of the topic, the context from previous discussions that you had with the model, and your knowledge of the person that is asking,” said Bhattacharjee. “So reasoning is where the model now does a next level of thinking and comes up with a better response. It&#8217;s more holistic in terms of covering a wider spectrum rather than just answering the question that is being asked.”</p>
<p>Reasoning models are also subject to training, so if a particular step in the reasoning was incorrect, that feedback can improve performance on future queries.</p>
<p>The reasoning element involves calculations better suited to GPUs than CPUs. “Reasoning is typically part of model inference and runs primarily on GPUs or other AI accelerators,” said Bhattacharjee. “Thinking involves generating additional tokens and neural-network computation that is best done by accelerators.”</p>
<p>Reasoning models have been commercially released. “OpenAI’s O-series models and DeepSeek-R1 are examples of commercially deployed reasoning models,” added Bhattacharjee.</p>
<p><strong>Crowdsourcing (or cloudsourcing?)<br />
</strong>LLMs are enormous models, and running each token through the entire model is resource-intensive. Two approaches attempt to tame the extent of these models.</p>
<p>The simple one is a small language model (SLM). Instead of trying to capture all of the internet and human knowledge in one model, it focuses on a specialty and is very well trained on that specialty, but on nothing else. An SLM is a self-contained model that can run independently.</p>
<p>Then, an increasingly popular technique segregates portions of individual model layers as experts in a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model. On a given layer, one can establish multiple experts that are independent of each other. Each has its own set of weights, making it better at dealing with certain tokens.</p>
<p>“Some of the model’s dense feed-forward network (FFN) layers are replaced by multiple separate FFNs, or ‘experts,’ together with a learned router,” explained Bhattacharjee.</p>
<p>“Earlier we had this scaling in large language models where if you just added more parameters, you got better performance,” explained Priyank Shukla, director of product management, interface IP at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/synopsys-inc/">Synopsys</a>. “With a mixture of experts, you not only have one large parameter model, but you have expert models, so you don&#8217;t need 10 trillion parameters for the whole process. You split it, and you have, let&#8217;s say, 1 trillion, which will do, let&#8217;s say, legal work. 1 trillion will do math work. And the front-end model will give the query to the right model.”</p>
<p>There&#8217;s a generic model that says, ‘Let me understand what question is being asked,’ called the pre-fill phase. “During that phase, it parses out your prompt to understand the context,&#8221; said Bhattacharjee. &#8220;Then there&#8217;s a series of experts that it works with. Once it understands that your question is related to, say, healthcare, there&#8217;s an expert trained on healthcare.”</p>
<p>A gating function or router decides, for a given token, which expert to send it to. Theoretically, it could send it to all experts, but typically only one or two get a shot at it. Training happens in the usual way, but the router is also trained by watching which experts perform best on different tokens during training. That allows it to direct tokens appropriately during inference.</p>
<p>The context reflecting everything that’s happened so far in the inference process is stored in the key-value cache (KV cache). It gets larger as processing continues and drives future decisions. This will be sent to the selected expert.</p>
<p>“We have to transmit the KV cache from the first model, which interacts with the relevant mixture of experts,” said Synopsys&#8217; Shukla.</p>
<p>The router also executes on the accelerators. “The routing or gating function is part of the model itself and generally executed on the accelerator alongside the model,” Bhattacharjee noted.</p>
<p>Finally, the segregation of experts happens at training. “The experts are trained jointly and aren’t normally manually assigned,” he said.</p>
<p>That distinction becomes clearer when MoE is compared directly with the other specialization strategy: small language models.</p>
<p><strong>SLMs vs. MoE<br />
</strong>SLMs and MoEs are distinct in two critical ways. SLMs can process an entire string of tokens, whereas a given expert will handle only certain tokens within a string. SLMs are smaller models and require fewer resources to run. MoEs make bigger models. An ordinary LLM would have only one expert (on everything), while an MoE provides multiple experts for the same task, making the model larger than its pure LLM equivalent. But it’s still likely smaller than what would be necessary if the entire model had to be trained to cover all areas without experts.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282673" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/SLM-vs.-MoE-Moyer.png?resize=434%2C263&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="434" height="263" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/SLM-vs.-MoE-Moyer.png?w=434&amp;ssl=1 434w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/SLM-vs.-MoE-Moyer.png?resize=300%2C182&amp;ssl=1 300w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 434px) 100vw, 434px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. </strong><strong>1</strong><strong>:</strong><strong> SLM vs. MoE. A specialized LLM can be condensed into an SLM, whereas a MoE model has multiple options for critical parts of the model, with a router that decides which “experts” will handle the next token. Source: Bryon Moyer/Semiconductor Engineering</strong></p>
<p>In addition, an MoE model can have broader coverage, with embedded experts covering a wide range of topics. An SLM covers only a narrow range and is therefore more limited in the material it can consume.</p>
<p>MoE models tend to be larger than regular “dense” models, because one critical feed-forward layer may be replaced by several experts. That means the total parameter count may exceed that of a standard model, but since only a few experts run at any given time, not all of those parameters need to be fetched.</p>
<p>“An MoE model can have a very large total parameter count because it contains multiple experts, but only a subset of those experts is activated for each token,” explained Bhattacharjee. “That sparse activation is the key advantage. It allows the model to increase its overall capacity without requiring every parameter to participate in every inference operation.”</p>
<p>Less clear are the power implications of MoE models. “Although an MoE model may contain more total parameters, only a subset of its experts is typically activated for each token,” said Bhattacharjee. “That means it can require less computation per token than a dense model with a comparable total parameter count. The tradeoff is that routing, memory access, and communication between devices can introduce additional overhead, so efficiency increasingly depends on the design of the overall system rather than parameter count alone.”</p>
<p><strong>Random reservoirs<br />
</strong>A rather obscure type of model is called reservoir computing. With a limited remit for handling time sequences, it’s much easier to train than typical models since most of the model is random. The training process affects only the last layer, which takes whatever the random bits produce and maps it to a correct answer.</p>
<p>“It’s a specialized approach for dynamic temporal inputs, particularly for low power, fast adoption, and where you know simple training is valuable,” said Bhattacharjee.</p>
<p>Because most of the model&#8217;s contents don’t matter, they can be hard-coded into silicon, with only the last layer accepting trained weights. It also requires far less energy since only weights for the last layer must be fetched.</p>
<p>Not much is heard about this type of AI, but it can be useful for speech or audio recognition, processing sensor data and controlling motors on robots, and modeling sequences, including time-series prediction for applications such as weather and financial markets.</p>
<p>Quantum Computing Inc. (QCI) has a photonic version of a reservoir computer being readied for launch. “You can implement reservoir computing using other methods, but among all the methods, photonics is one of the best choices because of the bandwidth,” said Prajnesh Kumar, quantum technology lead at QCI.</p>
<p>One benefit of photonics is that it can eventually use wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM) to boost productivity. “Say you have 10 wavelengths,” explained Kumar. “You can put 10 different tasks on these wavelengths. Then if your kernel is the same for all of them, you can perform 10 operations in parallel without any sort of interference.”</p>
<p>That way, they’re addressing specific tasks that require high performance and low power. “There are certain future applications such as vertical takeoff vehicles where you need to do trajectory planning,” said Kumar. “You don&#8217;t want vehicles to collide. I have also been talking to one of the professors who&#8217;s been using our previous-generation product to analyze brain signals and figure out whether we can classify epilepsy versus other conditions based on brain activity. There are other applications, more toward certain military and defense applications.”</p>
<p>Taken together, these specialized approaches broaden the AI landscape rather than pointing to a single dominant architecture.</p>
<p><strong>Many model types<br />
</strong>The number of different model types keeps evolving, and that’s unlikely to change anytime soon. Today, CNNs still have a home, while LLMs and agentic AI are the big powerhouses, with MoE now gaining traction. Reasoning models aren’t as widespread but have their niche, as does reservoir computing.</p>
<p>Most of these technologies continue to rely on GPUs (or other NPUs) for the heavy lifting. The big exception is agentic AI, which is putting a premium on CPUs while not removing any of the pressure on GPUs.</p>
<p>It remains to be seen whether new breakthroughs such as attention and transformers occur regularly, but for now, developers are running hard with what is available today to find better ways to use it—with no end in sight.</p>
<p><strong>Reference<br />
</strong>1. Michael te Vrugt, “An introduction to reservoir computing,&#8221; book chapter to appear in: Artificial Intelligence and Intelligent Matter, Springer, Cham, <span class="arxivid"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.13212v1">arXiv:2412.13212v1</a> </span></p>

Standalone GPUs are being replaced by heterogeneous SoCs and chiplets that combine CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs to eliminate memory bottlenecks, reduce latency, and boost efficiency.</p>

		<title>How Close Are We To Fully Autonomous Chip Design?</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/how-close-are-we-to-fully-autonomous-chip-design/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/how-close-are-we-to-fully-autonomous-chip-design/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Ed Sperling]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 15 Oct 2026 07:01:10 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Low Power-High Performance]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Top Stories]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[3D-IC]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[agentic AI]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[AI]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[autonomous chip design]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[IP]]></category>

		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24282785</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Synopsys CEO Sassine Ghazi talks about AI agents, the limits of autonomous engineering, digital twins, and the challenges facing 3D-ICs.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/how-close-are-we-to-fully-autonomous-chip-design/">How Close Are We To Fully Autonomous Chip Design?</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p><strong>Key Takeaways:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Autonomous chip design is advancing, but human engineers remain essential — at least for now.</li>
<li>Systems companies are pressuring EDA to shorten chip design cycles so they can keep pace with rapidly changing AI workloads.</li>
<li>Advanced packaging, physical AI, and digital twins require broader co-analysis and co-design for multiphysics.</li>
</ul>
<hr />
<p>Sassine Ghazi, president and CEO of <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/synopsys-inc/">Synopsys</a>, sat down with Semiconductor Engineering to discuss how AI is transforming chip design and engineering. What follows are excerpts from a keynote interview at SEMICON West this week, which was conducted before a live audience.</p>
<p><strong>SE: The big change over the past year, and really the big story right now, is AI. We&#8217;re processing more AI data. Chips need to run faster. They need to run cooler. Do we really need to rethink how we&#8217;re developing these chips?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Ghazi</strong>: Absolutely. Actually, we started talking about how to re-engineer engineering, because you need to co-design and optimize across multiple intersections, starting at the physics level, material, process technology, architecture, design, along with the software and the model itself, because the model itself is what&#8217;s defining the workload, and how do you optimize along that stack?</p>
<p><strong>SE: So where does AI actually fit into chip design? We&#8217;ve been dealing with computational software since what, the 1980s?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Ghazi</strong>: Yes. Around the 2016 time frame, we introduced reinforcement learning in a number of our technologies and tools to take advantage of a large space of parameters that you need to optimize, and to use AI to assist the human engineer in optimizing that large space. Today, we&#8217;ve moved from an assistant to an actual orchestration of multiple task agents. We have more than 40 task agents. Those task agents are experts of the tools, where you feed them all the knowledge, the capabilities that the tools need in order to optimize for a certain outcome. So those are specific task agents. The magic that has happened over the last year or so is the advancement in intelligence and reasoning of these models. You have long-horizon orchestration, where these models can orchestrate multiple agents, and all you have to do is give it an outcome you&#8217;re trying to achieve. That&#8217;s where we are today. So it is truly amazing the progress that we&#8217;ve made.</p>
<p><strong>SE: Where do you see this going? We&#8217;ve gone from GenAI over the past four years to Agentic AI. What comes next?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Ghazi</strong>: You can look at it this way. <img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="wp-image-24282786 alignleft" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-14-at-12.42.34-PM.png?resize=372%2C273&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="372" height="273" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-14-at-12.42.34-PM.png?w=1073&amp;ssl=1 1073w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-14-at-12.42.34-PM.png?resize=300%2C220&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-14-at-12.42.34-PM.png?resize=1024%2C752&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-14-at-12.42.34-PM.png?resize=768%2C564&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-14-at-12.42.34-PM.png?resize=600%2C441&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 372px) 100vw, 372px" />We started from an assistant copilot, to generative capability, to now what we&#8217;re describing as long-horizon autonomous agents, where instead of giving a prompt, you give an outcome, and you expect that model is able to reason and trigger actions for multiple agents to achieve that task. So it&#8217;s autonomous engineering. Now the question typically comes up then, &#8216;What happens to the human engineer? What is the role that they play, and is that a risk for the industry?&#8217; Actually, I don&#8217;t see it that way at all. Today, there&#8217;s a massive demand for more companies to define and specialize silicon, to customize silicon. And if you think about the challenges that the industry is having, it&#8217;s the shortage of human engineers to be able to architect, take a spec, define the silicon, and drive toward an outcome. So the whole autonomous orchestration is a very positive thing for the industry, where you still need the human judgment to define the architecture, to guide, and to sign off the final check before you go into product manufacturing.</p>
<p><strong>SE: At the Converged conference earlier this year, some of the big chipmakers said that they will be able to develop chips with no human in the loop. Is that realistic? And if so, where does the human play? Is it a matter of, &#8216;Check this, make sure it&#8217;s accurate, it actually works as I expect?&#8217;</strong></p>
<p><strong>Ghazi</strong>: That&#8217;s the ambition. Today, we do have a number of engagements and technologies where you can start with a spec. The spec comes from a system company. The system company can be — think of any hyperscaler, any frontier AI lab, any EV automotive, drone. Think of a system company defining a spec. That spec is based on the end product. At some point, you need to translate it into the electronic spec. Today, we have engagements where the customer can provide a spec to Synopsys Autonomous Agent, and it moves it to a verified RTL, which is the starting point for the chip design. That process used to take many months for many human engineers, to go from the spec to writing the RTL, verifying the RTL, and ensuring that it can be physically implemented and manufactured. So today we have that step being done autonomously. We have it. We have a number of customers engaged in it now. With the intelligence and the reasoning, can it expand into the physical implementation, physical verification, into the sign-off of the chip? I have no doubt we&#8217;ll get there. Is this here today? No. Is there an ambition to have more autonomy in that workflow? Absolutely.</p>
<p><strong>SE: So do agents now become the new IP?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Ghazi</strong>: Maybe a different way to ask the question is, &#8216;What will be the core IP for Synopsys? Is it the tool itself? Is it the agent who is the expert on the tool and needs the tool in order to perform a task?&#8217; So today, the model is fantastic at reasoning and exploring. You still need the tool, i.e., the agent, in order to generate and to validate. Because you can generate an outcome, you can explore many design options and possibilities. But at the end, you have to decide on one implementation that provides the best performance, power, cost, etc.</p>
<p><strong>SE: The reason I ask that question is that when Synopsys was developing — and still is developing — IP, almost all of that ended up as custom IP because your customers demanded that it fit into something. Do AI agents now fill that because they do adapt?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Ghazi</strong>: There is what I describe as the classic EDA products — the tools used for design. And then there&#8217;s the IP, which is the interface IP. These are needed to connect chip-to-chip and the chip to the system. Those are increasingly customized. Let&#8217;s say you&#8217;re a hyperscaler. You&#8217;re trying to optimize your chip and customize it for a specific workload in order to achieve performance, power targets, etc. If the interface IP is general, and not customized, then you&#8217;re losing competitiveness. The area may not be optimized. The performance is not optimized because it&#8217;s general-purpose IP.</p>
<p><strong>SE: Changing topics, there&#8217;s a whole new market opening up in physical AI, but there&#8217;s a lot of dependencies that you have to think about. There&#8217;s a lot of data orchestration, and it&#8217;s a brand new opportunity. Elon Musk was promoting this as a $25 trillion to $30 trillion opportunity [just for Tesla] as we go forward. What do you see?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Ghazi</strong>: As AI expands from digital to physical, the silicon is powering both. You need customized silicon for both. The moment you start moving to physical application, it&#8217;s software-defined. The automotive industry has been heading down that path for at least 7 to 10 years with the software-defined vehicle. As the vehicle becomes autonomous, you need to model not only the electronics and the physics of the end product. You need to model for the environment in which it&#8217;s operating. So it&#8217;s a multiple optimization opportunity between silicon, the system itself — that includes multiple engineering of structure, fluid, the actual mechanical system — and how to model the environment in which that system is going to operate. So it&#8217;s a massive engineering opportunity, and we play from the silicon to the system. The system is through the acquisition of Ansys. We have the multi-physics sign-off. If you want to sign off either a chip or an end system, i.e., a car, a robot, anything that is an intelligent system, you need to make sure that you&#8217;re not overdesigning the product. You&#8217;re not overbuilding it. So how do you design it just right and be able to sign off across multiple physics before you commit to manufacturing?</p>
<p><strong>SE: And this isn&#8217;t just a system of systems. It&#8217;s a system of heterogeneous systems, right?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Ghazi</strong>: Yes. The hardest part for me to describe is the definition of &#8216;system&#8217; at multiple levels of abstraction, because an advanced package is a system. But that&#8217;s a component when you start thinking of a rack. It becomes a component as you&#8217;re thinking of a subsystem or a data center. So it&#8217;s a different level of abstraction of a system.</p>
<p><strong>SE: One of the ways that people have talked about controlling AI — and we&#8217;ve all heard the stories about escapes from sandboxes — is with digital twins. We&#8217;ve been hearing about digital twins for probably a decade at this point. Has anybody actually produced one? And if not, what&#8217;s the problem?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Ghazi</strong>: The concept of digital twin or virtualization has existed for a very long time. Actually, Synopsys made two acquisitions about 15 or 17 years ago in virtualizing chips, meaning creating a digital twin for a chip in order for the customer to start designing software before the chip is manufactured. So it gives the customer optionality of models to determine which chip is most appropriate for the system. Now, if you go to the system or a digital twin of a whole car, we do have customers that are able to create a digital twin for the entire electronics — a digital twin to do crash testing for the material and the structure and the physics of the car, so you don&#8217;t have to do physical prototypes and crash testing. There are parts of digital twins for different engineering domains. Today customers are using it. But is there a digital twin that encompasses the electronics, the physics, the environment in which that system operates, that today is available and broadly used by customers? Not really. But that&#8217;s part of the journey. And I&#8217;m not sure how you can build a future sophisticated intelligent system without having a digital twin. It will take you forever, and the cost will be astronomical.</p>
<p><strong>SE: But it&#8217;s still the classic divide-and-conquer, right?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Ghazi</strong>: Yes, because unless you&#8217;re starting completely from scratch, you typically start from the prior design and architecture, and you move to the next one. The one place I&#8217;m always amazed at, because they started from scratch, is China when it comes to robotics and EVs. There are many customers I visit in China, where the whole company started two or three years ago, and they started with a fully digital approach for design. The silicon just taped out, they put it on a board, they put it in a car or whatever the end system is, and the software is running within weeks. That&#8217;s a transformation in the way our customers are doing engineering. So is it possible? The answer is yes. But what are the constraints and the starting point in order to motivate an established engineering company to jump into that new way of working?</p>
<p><strong>SE: And also, where in the lifecycle of a car does this actually play? Because this takes an enormous amount of computing.</strong></p>
<p><strong>Ghazi</strong>: Yes, but if you think of the traditional OEMs, they create a new platform every four or six years — the platform meaning the whole car itself. The example I just gave happens every nine months to a year. So it&#8217;s almost at the same rhythm where as they&#8217;re updating the electronics, they&#8217;re updating the whole car. Of course, it takes a lot of compute investment, but at the end, net-net, your end product is more differentiated and you are at a much faster rhythm and pace of innovation.</p>
<p><strong>SE: And you&#8217;re also monitoring the health of these systems as they go forward too, right? Can you imagine a 3 nanometer chip lasting 15 years in a car?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Ghazi</strong>: The more you architect the system as individual components, where you&#8217;re able to validate it as a whole system, then it does give you the optionality based on cost, based on supply chain, based on many, many vectors that you can optimize.</p>
<p><strong>SE: Let&#8217;s shift topics here. 2026 was supposed to be the year of the 3D-IC. Is it real?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Ghazi</strong>: Yes. There are many chips sitting in data centers today that are 3D-ICs. It&#8217;s complex. There are challenges beyond the electronics where customers and manufacturing are struggling. It&#8217;s not the architecture of the electronics. It&#8217;s the physics and mechanical effects of that 3D-IC. What&#8217;s happening as you&#8217;re running the workload at a high level of intensity, and as it&#8217;s intended, is that you&#8217;re running into thermal [issues] inside the package. It&#8217;s causing some of the chiplets to warp or to crack. So it&#8217;s a mechanical challenge. The industry is absolutely working toward addressing it early, during the architecture of the 3D-IC, along with the workload that is running on them. That was actually the key thesis for Synopsys to acquire Ansys — how do we bring that physics simulation early during the design phase so you can take this into account, because absolutely the future is a heterogeneous integration of multiple chips.</p>
<p><strong>SE: And it&#8217;s a programming nightmare, because now you&#8217;ve got things like, &#8216;Okay, we&#8217;re going to have a spike in heat, we&#8217;re going to have a spike in this computing, and the spike is going to occur every 3 milliseconds.&#8217; So now, what do we do in between those 3 milliseconds? How do we cool it down?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Ghazi</strong>: Yes, actually, this is where I mentioned the workload. Designing and architecting the system, the advanced package and multi-die system, with the context of the workload becomes very essential. This is where many surprises happen in the field, where there&#8217;s a corner case you did not take into account, and that system overheats and breaks. So it&#8217;s an optimization along the stack, from the software to architecting the actual package, to implementing it, and taking into account both the physics and the design.</p>
<p><strong>SE: Let&#8217;s add one more element in here, which is that the AI itself may be changing as well. So you go back and think of what you were running in Gen AI, or you&#8217;re running in agentic AI, and now the queries are getting more complicated, as well.</strong></p>
<p><strong>Ghazi</strong>: And that&#8217;s why you have every system company trying to take control over their silicon development. It&#8217;s not because the semiconductor industry is not doing a fantastic job to optimize their silicon to a specific workload. But at the pace in which things are moving, the model is changing every three to four months. You cannot have silicon being updated every two to three years. And many of our semiconductor customers are pushing to reduce it from 18 months, 16 months, 14 months, to a year. Many of the system companies are pushing us to say how we can leverage AI and change the spec-to-tape-out to shorter than a year, shorter than nine months? Where are the bottlenecks? How can we design silicon that is very specific for a workload that we&#8217;re defining?</p>
<p><strong>SE: Or one that can adapt as you go forward, right?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Ghazi</strong>: Yes, the whole programmability of either a chiplet or the entire chip itself is the direction, but I&#8217;m not seeing it adopted too much by system companies compared to, &#8216;I need the speed in defining a spec and customizing that silicon.&#8217; And by the way, that silicon lifecycle is not more than two years to three years, so it&#8217;s not like they&#8217;re customizing it with the intention of keeping it for multiple generations of a model. So it&#8217;s the ability to optimize and deliver to the silicon at a much faster pace, and [for] the life of that silicon, it&#8217;s okay for it to be at a much shorter duration sitting in whatever application that they&#8217;re driving.</p>
<p><strong>SE: Given all this change, what worries you? What keeps you up at night?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Ghazi</strong>: The pace, the pace, the pace. You know, there&#8217;s a massive complexity that is going on. In our industry, we&#8217;ve collectively done an amazing job to innovate and to really deliver magic. I&#8217;ve never seen a pace and system-level co-design and complexity [like] what we&#8217;re dealing with right now. The companies that are able to transform from a classical traditional workflow to adopting that next workflow — it&#8217;s very easy to put it on a PowerPoint slide [but] it&#8217;s very hard for a company to deliver the current commitment to their customer and transform that same engineering workforce to deliver that future of intelligence married with the physics married with the product differentiation that each company is trying to deliver.</p>
<p><strong>SE: Does it make it hard to figure out where to place your bets? If you look at EDA, it has always exceeded almost every other hardware company that&#8217;s out there in terms of how much investment [as a percentage of revenue] you put into R&amp;D.</strong></p>
<p><strong>Ghazi</strong>: As a percentage of revenue, yes, EDA has always had the need to invest a bigger and bigger percentage of revenue to keep up. There is an opportunity with AI. I have not seen yet that it&#8217;s able to tame it [to be able to] say right now the investment will go down. So the investment that we&#8217;re making is actually continuing to increase, not decrease.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/how-close-are-we-to-fully-autonomous-chip-design/">How Close Are We To Fully Autonomous Chip Design?</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

		<title>Thermal Co-Simulation Testing Of Co-Packaged Optics</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/thermal-co-simulation-testing-of-co-packaged-optics/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/thermal-co-simulation-testing-of-co-packaged-optics/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Vladimir Stojanovic]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 15 Oct 2026 07:01:01 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Blogs - LPHP]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Co-Packaged Optics Insights]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Low Power-High Performance]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[advanced packaging]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Ayar Labs]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[co-packaged optics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[CPO]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Global Unichip Corp]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[multi-chip assembly]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[thermal]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[thermal simulation]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24282800</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Ensuring optical engines can operate reliably alongside high-power AI processors in multi-chip packages.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/thermal-co-simulation-testing-of-co-packaged-optics/">Thermal Co-Simulation Testing Of Co-Packaged Optics</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p><strong>By Vladimir Stojanovic and Igor Elkanovich</strong></p>
<p>The CPO revolution is at our doorstep. But transforming data center interconnects requires overcoming new challenges in architecture, power delivery, mechanical design, and thermal management. Of these, thermal management has emerged as one of the most critical areas for successfully deploying <a href="https://ayarlabs.com/glossary/co-packaged-optics-cpo/">co-packaged optics</a> (CPO) in hyperscale AI environments.</p>
<p>Thermal instability has been a concern for CPO technology. Ayar Labs and Global Unichip Corp. (GUC) jointly conducted thermal co-simulation of the advanced package design and determined the thermal floor map for the package and subsequent chiplets, including air- and liquid-cooled environments.</p>
<p>Since thermal stability has been raised as a concern for micro-ring-based CPO, we want to address it head-on. Our co-simulation data show that CPO can operate reliably within the thermal envelope of advanced multi-chip packages. We’re sharing these results to give hyperscalers the confidence to move forward with CPO deployments at scale.</p>
<h2>Novel design enables over 100 Tbps speeds</h2>
<p>Let’s start with the new <a href="https://ayarlabs.com/glossary/multi-chip-package-mcp/">multi-chip package</a> (MCP) design that integrates Ayar Labs’ TeraPHY optical engines into GUC’s advanced packaging and ASIC workflow. The new XPU MCP design replaces traditional electrical interconnects with Ayar Labs’ optical engines, which are attached directly to the MCP organic substrate. This architecture enables a full-duplex optical interface of more than 100 Tbps from the XPU package, an improvement of more than an order of magnitude over current XPUs.</p>
<p>UCIe-S provides bandwidth between the optical engines and the I/O chiplets over the MCP substrate. UCIe-A, on the other hand, is used for communication between the I/O chiplet and the main AI die over local silicon interconnect (LSI) bridges.</p>
<p>The scale of this design creates thermal challenges we must address. The complete package measures 105mm x 140mm, housing:</p>
<ul>
<li>2 XPUs (25.69mm x 32.40mm each)</li>
<li>8 HBM4 memory modules</li>
<li>4 I/O chiplets</li>
<li>8 TeraPHY optical engines (12.5mm x 13.0mm each)</li>
</ul>
<p>The +3 kW power envelope in a single package underscores the importance of thermal management and the need for optical engines to operate reliably alongside high-power AI processors. This complex multi-chip architecture requires sophisticated packaging. The design uses a 9-2-9 layer substrate structure to handle the complex routing requirements.</p>
<p>The design also addresses signal and power integrity challenges associated with the large-scale package. We perform thermal optimization at the XPU MCP level, while a stiffener design incorporates optical engines’ requirements and enables detachable fiber connections that meet mechanical stress and warpage requirements.</p>
<h2>What is thermal co-simulation and why is it important?</h2>
<p>Thermal co-simulation is the combined simulation of electrical behavior and heat flow across a chip. It lets designers predict temperatures, hotspots, and reliability issues in integrated circuits (ICs) and packages under realistic operating conditions. The data ensures the entire system operates within required temperature specifications. This is critical for successful deployment.</p>
<p>In GUC’s thermal integrity design flow, we consider every chip’s power maps and perform thermal crosstalk and dynamic thermal co-simulation to ensure the MCP’s thermal integrity from early-stage through sign-off. This allows us to identify local thermal hotspots and the impact of thermal crosstalk on the optical engine.</p>
<p>Thermal co-simulation is crucial for GUC’s advanced ASIC workflows. In our joint analysis, the MCP includes multiple chiplets to analyze thermal crosstalk between adjacent chiplet dies. Any heat generated by the entire interposer complex may affect the optical engine’s performance.</p>
<p>Thermal modeling is needed to optimize optical engine performance. This joint technical exercise deliberately probes thermal hotspots and thermal crosstalk to evaluate overall CPO thermal stability in a realistic customer package form factor. Rather than avoiding the hard questions, we designed the simulation to stress the system and raise any potential concerns.</p>
<p>These findings are invaluable for assessing advanced packaging designs and collaborating with ecosystem partners to design optimal cooling solutions for AI server and switch applications at the most demanding Thermal Design Power levels. This testing allows us to do just that.</p>
<h2>Thermal co‑sim testing</h2>
<p>We performed three simulations: an analysis to determine thermal resistance targets for each chip component, plus testing of two different cooling solutions. One solution met spec, and one did not.</p>
<h3>3D VC heatsink test</h3>
<p>We tested a standard air fin heatsink at airspeeds of 5 m/s and 6 m/s at 25ºC.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282801" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Ayar_Thermal-Co-Simulation-Testing-of-CPO-fig1.webp?resize=1920%2C1081&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1920" height="1081" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Ayar_Thermal-Co-Simulation-Testing-of-CPO-fig1.webp?w=1920&amp;ssl=1 1920w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Ayar_Thermal-Co-Simulation-Testing-of-CPO-fig1.webp?resize=300%2C169&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Ayar_Thermal-Co-Simulation-Testing-of-CPO-fig1.webp?resize=1024%2C577&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Ayar_Thermal-Co-Simulation-Testing-of-CPO-fig1.webp?resize=768%2C432&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Ayar_Thermal-Co-Simulation-Testing-of-CPO-fig1.webp?resize=1536%2C865&amp;ssl=1 1536w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Ayar_Thermal-Co-Simulation-Testing-of-CPO-fig1.webp?resize=600%2C338&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 1: GUC + Ayar Labs CoWoS-L CPO simulation using heatsink.</strong></p>
<p>This did not meet spec, as the temperature significantly exceeded spec for all components except the I/O die.</p>
<h3>Thermal resistance analysis</h3>
<p>We analyzed the maximum junction temperature versus resistance curve to determine suitable resistance for the Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate with Local Silicon Interconnect (CoWoS-L) advanced packaging and optical engine to meet the temperature spec.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282802" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Ayar_Thermal-Co-Simulation-Testing-of-CPO-fig2.webp?resize=1920%2C1081&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1920" height="1081" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Ayar_Thermal-Co-Simulation-Testing-of-CPO-fig2.webp?w=1920&amp;ssl=1 1920w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Ayar_Thermal-Co-Simulation-Testing-of-CPO-fig2.webp?resize=300%2C169&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Ayar_Thermal-Co-Simulation-Testing-of-CPO-fig2.webp?resize=1024%2C577&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Ayar_Thermal-Co-Simulation-Testing-of-CPO-fig2.webp?resize=768%2C432&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Ayar_Thermal-Co-Simulation-Testing-of-CPO-fig2.webp?resize=1536%2C865&amp;ssl=1 1536w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Ayar_Thermal-Co-Simulation-Testing-of-CPO-fig2.webp?resize=600%2C338&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 2: GUC + Ayar Labs CoWoS-L CPO Thermal Resistance (Rsa) analysis.</strong></p>
<p>The system-level thermal solution successfully meets the specification when RSA-ASIC is ≤ 0.008 K/W and RSA-OE is ≤ 0.15 K/W. The cold plate design achieves these targets with pressure drops of 11.2 kPa for the ASIC cold plate and 18.8 kPa for the optical engine cold plate. This ensures efficient coolant flow while maintaining thermal performance.</p>
<h3>Cold plate test</h3>
<p>Finally, we tested an impingement-type cold plate thermal solution at 4.5 LPM.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282803" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Ayar_Thermal-Co-Simulation-Testing-of-CPO-fig3.webp?resize=1920%2C1081&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1920" height="1081" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Ayar_Thermal-Co-Simulation-Testing-of-CPO-fig3.webp?w=1920&amp;ssl=1 1920w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Ayar_Thermal-Co-Simulation-Testing-of-CPO-fig3.webp?resize=300%2C169&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Ayar_Thermal-Co-Simulation-Testing-of-CPO-fig3.webp?resize=1024%2C577&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Ayar_Thermal-Co-Simulation-Testing-of-CPO-fig3.webp?resize=768%2C432&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Ayar_Thermal-Co-Simulation-Testing-of-CPO-fig3.webp?resize=1536%2C865&amp;ssl=1 1536w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Ayar_Thermal-Co-Simulation-Testing-of-CPO-fig3.webp?resize=600%2C338&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 3: GUC + Ayar Labs CoWoS-L CPO simulation using cold plate.</strong></p>
<p>This solution did meet spec. All components were below the temperature specifications.</p>
<h2>Cold plate details</h2>
<p>We selected the impingement-type cold plate for this application because it enables higher heat flux removal than conventional parallel-channel designs. The design uses optimized fin dimensions (thickness: 0.15mm, height: 2.4mm for the ASIC and 3.0mm for the optical engine) with thermal interface materials (K=5.2 W/mK) to achieve the required thermal performance.</p>
<p>This approach effectively dissipates the concentrated heat from multiple high-power chiplets while maintaining the optical engines within their operational temperature limits.</p>
<p>Key Results</p>
<ul>
<li>Determined the thermal resistance design targets for each chiplet for thermal sign-off constraints:
<ul>
<li>HBM4 &lt; 95ºC</li>
<li>SoC &lt; 125ºC</li>
<li>Optical Engine &lt; 100ºC</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Mapped the location of thermal hotspots.</li>
<li>Showed that a traditional air heatsink does not work for this solution.</li>
<li>Demonstrated that a real-world liquid cooling device meets the specifications needed.</li>
</ul>
<p>These results point to a significant breakthrough in CPO deployment. Successfully maintaining optical engines under 100ºC while dissipating over 3kW TDP from a single package (with 1,500W coming from the AI processors alone) shows that CPO operates reliably with ample junction-temperature headroom, paving the way for the most demanding thermal environments.</p>
<h2>Future plans</h2>
<p>Our next step will focus on dynamic workload simulation to further analyze thermal impact on CPO under real-world operating conditions. The tests we’ve shared here were based on static power assumptions, where each component’s power consumption remains constant. Systems ramp up from idle, spike during training or booting, and fluctuate based on user demand during normal operations.</p>
<p>Large numbers of users can cause heat spikes. A dynamic workload simulation will allow us to test our design under conditions more accurate to the real world. This will help us understand how the optics respond to sudden temperature changes and ensure the systems operate efficiently.</p>
<p>These thermal co-simulation test results demonstrate that CPO can operate reliably in high-power AI systems when paired with appropriate cooling solutions. As the industry continues to push the boundaries of compute performance and thermal design power, CPO will play a significant role in overcoming bandwidth and power limitations.</p>
<p><em>Igor Elkanovich is the CTO of GUC.</em></p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/thermal-co-simulation-testing-of-co-packaged-optics/">Thermal Co-Simulation Testing Of Co-Packaged Optics</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Researchers at <strong>ETH Zürich</strong> and <strong>New York University</strong> published a technical paper titled “Understanding the Power Consumption of Modern High Bandwidth Memory: Experimental Analysis and Modeling Using Real HBM2 DRAM Chips.&#8221;</p>
<p><strong>Abstract Excerpt:</strong></p>
<p>“We perform the first comprehensive experimental characterization of power consumed by real HBM2 DRAM chips. Our extensive characterization yields 1) the empirical basis for developing new, accurate HBM power models or validating existing power models and 2) key insights into structural and data-pattern-dependent variation of power in HBM2 chips. Out of our 13 new findings and 6 key takeaway messages, we highlight: 1) a read operation consumes significantly higher current than any other operation and 2) the toggled data bus signals in a data transfer burst significantly affect current draw where toggling all HBM2-internal bank group bus signals causes 29.4% higher power consumption than keeping them constant. Leveraging our empirical insights into HBM2 power consumption, we engineer an access pattern that yields 23.6% higher power consumption on average across 36 tested HBM2 chips than the highest-power-consuming JEDEC-specified current measurement loop.&#8221;</p>
<p>Find the <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14244">technical paper here</a>. October 2026.</p>
<p>Olgun, Ataberk, Spiros Galanopoulos, Andreas Kosmas Kakolyris, İsmail Emir Yüksel, Haocong Luo, F. Nisa Bostancı, and Onur Mutlu. “Understanding the Power Consumption of Modern High Bandwidth Memory: Experimental Analysis and Modeling Using Real HBM2 DRAM Chips.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2610.14244 (October 2026). https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.14244</p>
<p>&nbsp;</p>

<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/simulations-pinpoint-leakage-pathway-in-gaafets-sandia-luxembourg/">Simulations Pinpoint Leakage Pathway In GAAFETs (Sandia, Luxembourg)</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Researchers at <strong>Sandia National Laboratories</strong> and <strong>Luxembourg Institute of Science and Technology</strong> published a technical paper titled “Revealing New Leakage Paths in GAAFETs using Predictive First-Principles Simulations.”</p>
<p><strong>Abstract Excerpt:</strong></p>
<p>“Gate-All-Around Field-Effect Transistors (GAAFETs) are emerging as successors to Fin Field-Effect Transistors (FinFETs) and are central to continued scaling at advanced semiconductor nodes. Despite their improved electrostatic control, recent measurements show that the drain current in GAAFETs deviates strongly from thermionic behavior at negative gate voltages, increasing as the gate voltage becomes more negative. This leakage has been attributed to direct gate-drain tunneling through the high-<span id="MathJax-Element-1-Frame" class="MathJax" tabindex="0"><span id="MathJax-Span-1" class="math"><span id="MathJax-Span-2" class="mrow"><span id="MathJax-Span-3" class="mi">k</span></span></span></span> dielectric, enhanced by drain-induced dielectric barrier lowering (DIDBL). Here, we use predictive, charge-self-consistent Non-Equilibrium Green Function (NEGF) simulations based on the Contact Block Reduction (CBR) method to spatially resolve this leakage pathway in GAAFETs.”</p>
<p>Find the <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14298">technical paper here</a>. October 2026.</p>
<p>Mamaluy, Denis, Juan P. Mendez, Coleman Cariker, Michael Titze, and Alex A. Belianinov. “Revealing New Leakage Paths in GAAFETs using Predictive First-Principles Simulations.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2610.14298 (October 2026). https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.14298. Creative Commons <a href="https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">license.</a></p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-medium wp-image-24282781" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-14-at-10.44.39-AM.png?resize=300%2C268&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="300" height="268" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-14-at-10.44.39-AM.png?resize=300%2C268&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-14-at-10.44.39-AM.png?resize=1024%2C916&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-14-at-10.44.39-AM.png?resize=768%2C687&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-14-at-10.44.39-AM.png?resize=600%2C536&amp;ssl=1 600w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-14-at-10.44.39-AM.png?w=1114&amp;ssl=1 1114w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 300px) 100vw, 300px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig.1: GAAFET architecture and cross-sectional schematic of the single-sheet GAAFET device used in this work. <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14298">Source</a>: Revealing New Leakage Paths in GAAFETs using Predictive First-Principles Simulations</strong></p>
